_about: THE single source of truth for what Dhar can do today. Edit this file, run `python3 status/render.py`, commit the result. The website board, the README status block, the speed tables and the progress log are generated from it (and from benchmarks/results/*.json), and tests/test_status.py fails if any of them has drifted or if a claim here no longer matches the code. Text fields use `backticks` for code. Statuses: works | partly | designed | notyet. See docs/HONESTY.md for what each word means.

components.title: Stage 0 compiler
components.text: `dharc` is written in NASM x86-64 assembly (nine modules, no libc). It reads a `.dhar` file and writes assembly; `nasm` and a linker turn that into a program. The conformance battery has {battery_total} tests and all of them pass on both targets.

components.title: Native programs, no runtime
components.text: Output is a small static program that talks to the operating system directly: `gen` and `sys` both end in a system call, with no library between. The examples below are about 9 KB each.

components.title: Bounds checking on buffers
components.text: An index outside a `raw[N]` buffer stops the program with `Dhar: index out of bounds` and exit status 1, instead of silently corrupting memory.

components.title: The language itself
components.text: A strict first subset: `i32`, `str`, `bool` and `raw[N]`; type inference from the first value (`lock x = 5`); tasks with parameters; `give` with a value or one operation (`give a + b`); `gen(...)` to print a string, a number or an `i32`, `str` or `bool` variable; `when`/`shift`/`fallback`; loops; `sys` calls; layout-only `mold`. Anything outside the subset is rejected with a clear message. Known limit: a global variable cannot have an initial value yet (assign it inside a task); the compiler says so instead of silently ignoring it.

components.title: Target: Linux x86-64
components.text: Programs are built, linked and run natively in the tests.

components.title: Target: Windows x64
components.text: Programs assemble as win64, link into a PE, and run correctly in a CPU emulator that checks the Windows calling rules; all {battery_total} tests pass there. It has not been run on a real Windows machine yet, and `dharc` itself still runs only on Linux (on Windows, use WSL).

components.title: Targets: ARM64, RISC-V, WebAssembly (WASI)
components.text: `dharc` refuses these with an error rather than producing the wrong output. The author decided on 23 October 2026 to build them in Stage 0 itself (not postpone them to Stage 1); nothing of that is built yet, and each target is switched on only when the whole test battery passes on it. The Canon still says Stage 0 targets x86-64 only, so the decision needs Canon amendment A-2.

components.title: Stage 1: the compiler written in Dhar
components.text: {stage1_files} source files exist in the Honing Dhar repository (lexer, parser, AST, symbols, type check, IR, code generation, driver) and all of them pass through Stage 0. They are scaffolding and stubs, not a working compiler.

components.title: Safety without a garbage collector
components.text: Compile-time ownership and borrowing (`view`, `grab`) and the error model (`state`, `trap`, `enforce`) are specified. Stage 0 rejects them; there is no borrow checker yet.

components.title: Cybersecurity, AI and quantum direction
components.text: The direction and its acceptance gates are written down as Canon Amendment A-1, a draft that still needs the author's ratification. Nothing for them is built yet: no `std.crypto`, no float or tensor types, no quantum back end.

components.title: Self-hosting
components.text: Stage 1 does not compile itself, so the byte-for-byte bootstrap check has not been run.

components.title: Optimiser
components.text: Every variable lives in memory and nothing is kept in registers. That is the main reason Dhar trails C in the speed test. Register allocation is planned for after the bootstrap.

components.title: Modules, standard library, `Kun`
components.text: `pull` and `expose` are validated but link a single file. There is no importer, no standard library and no package manager yet; programs call the system directly.

components.title: Try Dhar in the browser
components.text: Planned for this website. It needs a way to run `dharc` and the result in the browser, and nothing of that exists yet.

pipeline.title: Stage 0, the bridge
pipeline.text: Reads Dhar, writes assembly. The blueprint named C for the bridge; the one that exists is written directly in NASM assembly.

pipeline.title: Stage 1, the compiler in Dhar
pipeline.text: The lexer, parser, type checker, IR and code generator, all written in Dhar itself and using only what Stage 0 accepts. Scaffolding exists; the compiler does not yet.

pipeline.title: Hand-off
pipeline.text: Stage 0 compiles the Stage 1 source. The result is the first compiler built from Dhar's own code.

pipeline.title: Self-host check
pipeline.text: That compiler compiles the Stage 1 source again. If the logic is sound, the two executables are byte-for-byte identical.

pipeline.title: Independence
pipeline.text: Stage 0 is archived. After that, optimisation, a standard library and tooling are built on Dhar itself.

tracks_intro: Security first, then AI, then quantum. None of this is built. It starts after Stage 1 compiles itself; until then the work is to leave room for it in the design. Each line below is a gate: a test that must pass before the line is called done.

tracks.name: Cybersecurity
tracks.why: Dhar already starts from the right place: no libc, no runtime, a compiler small enough to read, and bounds checks that stop an out-of-range write.

gates.text: Memory safety floor. Every index is checked (this works today for `raw[N]`), and ownership and borrowing (`view`, `grab`) are enforced at compile time, with no garbage collector.
Constant-time code. Values marked secret may not decide a branch or an array index, and the compiler may not rewrite them into one.

A first `std.crypto`: SHA-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305, X25519 and Ed25519, each passing its published test vectors (FIPS 180-4, RFC 8439, RFC 7748, RFC 8032) and a timing test that shows no input-dependent variation.
A build you can trust. Stage 1 compiles itself byte for byte, two machines produce identical output from the same source, and every build lists what went into it.

tracks.name: Artificial intelligence
tracks.why: Models are numbers in arrays. A language with checked bounds, no garbage collector and no runtime can run them with a memory use that is known before they start.

gates.text: Numbers for models: `f32` and `f64`, fixed-point, and SIMD vector types, with results checked against a reference implementation.
Tensors without a garbage collector: fixed-shape arrays and views with checked bounds, and arena allocation.
Inference end to end: a small trained network (a handwritten-digit classifier) runs from a Dhar program with no outside runtime, and its outputs match a reference framework to a stated tolerance.
Measured speed: the gap to optimised C on matrix multiply and on that network is published, whatever it is. GPUs and other accelerators come after this, not before.

tracks.name: Quantum computing
tracks.why: Two separate needs: protecting today's data from future quantum computers, which needs no quantum hardware, and describing and simulating quantum programs.

gates.text: Post-quantum cryptography: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), each passing the NIST known-answer tests.
Circuits as data: a Dhar program builds a quantum circuit and writes it as OpenQASM 3 that a reference tool accepts.
A state-vector simulator written in Dhar, checked against a reference simulator on a fixed set of circuits.
Real quantum hardware stays out of scope until Q2 and Q3 pass and a provider's interface allows it.

milestones.title: Website, survey and Canon moved to their own repository
milestones.text: The website, the survey (now a page of the website, at /survey/), the Canon documents and the progress reports live in one branch of the Dhar-website-and-docs repository, served from Render at https://dhar.onrender.com instead of GitHub Pages. This replaces the GitHub Pages step in Progress Report 001. The survey saves answers in a Supabase database; its table rules were checked on PostgreSQL (36 checks) and the page against an imitation of the service, but not yet against the live project.

milestones.title: Buffer address in `scan` fixed
milestones.text: Checking the Stage 1 sources against the compiler turned up a wrong stack offset: for `scan` over a local buffer the compiler wrote the buffer's address as `rbp-4294967336` instead of `rbp-40`. `nasm` warned and cut the number down to the right value, so programs printed the right answer and nothing visibly failed. The compiler now writes the right offset; two new tests check the output and the assembly text, and the assembly test fails on the previous compiler. {battery_total} tests pass on both targets.

milestones.title: `gen(...)` is the print function
milestones.text: Printing no longer needs a buffer and a raw system call: `gen("text")`, `gen(42)` and `gen(name)` write a string, a number or a variable, for variables declared with a type and for ones whose type was inferred (`lock x = 5`). `gen` is strict: parentheses, exactly one argument, and a name that is an `i32`, `str` or `bool`. While testing it, a global `flux g: i32 = 77` turned out to be silently ignored (the variable stayed 0); the compiler now rejects it with a message, and it is listed as a limit, not fixed. {battery_total} tests pass on both targets; the new tests fail on the previous compiler.

milestones.title: Negative literals in `give`
milestones.text: Checking the Stage 1 sources against the new compiler showed that `give -1` had always compiled as `give 0` (a silent miscompile) and that the first version of the `give` fix rejected it. It now returns the negative number, with 68 tests passing on both targets.

milestones.title: Windows x64 target
milestones.text: Stage 0 emits real Windows programs; unsupported targets are refused instead of silently producing Linux code. The battery grew to 64 tests and passes on both targets.

milestones.title: Two Stage 0 bugs fixed
milestones.text: `give a + b` used to return only `a`; `gen("...")` used to write an extra zero byte. Both fixed, with 14 tests that fail on the old compiler.

milestones.title: Direction written down
milestones.text: Canon Amendment A-1, a draft awaiting ratification, proposes the order: cybersecurity, then artificial intelligence, then quantum computing, each with test gates. Nothing for them is built yet.

milestones.title: Honest status in one place
milestones.text: One status file now drives the website, the README and the progress log, and a test fails if any of them drifts from it.

milestones.title: Website and logo
milestones.text: The DHAR logo and brand rules were fixed (six colours, two typefaces), and the first version of this site was built with code samples run on the real compiler. Running them also exposed the two Stage 0 bugs fixed on 22 October.

milestones.title: Stage 0 split into nine modules
milestones.text: The monolithic source was divided into one-definition-per-file modules.
